title: Career Roadmap · Electro-Technical Officer (ETO)
summary: ETO duties differ from those of a marine engineer. The ETO primarily focuses on electrical, electronic and control systems, while the engineering department has broader responsibility for mechanical propulsion and machinery operations.

facts.Current degree: Merchant Navy / Maritime Programmes – Electro-Technical Officer (ETO) Course

about.label: Primary Sector
about.text: Merchant Shipping, Offshore Operations, Ship Management

about.label: Work Environment
about.text: Engine rooms, electrical workshops, control rooms and shipboard technical spaces

about.label: Typical Entry Route
about.text: Relevant electrical/electronics education → Approved ETO training → Required onboard training and certification

about.label: Long-Term Progression
about.text: ETO → Senior ETO / Electrical Technical Specialist → Fleet Electrical Superintendent or Technical Manager, subject to experience and employer requirements

blocks.label: Career overview
blocks.text: An Electro-Technical Officer maintains and troubleshoots a ship's electrical, electronic, automation and control systems. The role is essential to the safe operation of propulsion-support systems, power generation, navigation equipment, communication systems and shipboard automation.

ETO duties differ from those of a marine engineer. The ETO primarily focuses on electrical, electronic and control systems, while the engineering department has broader responsibility for mechanical propulsion and machinery operations.

An ETO works with shipboard electrical distribution, generators, motors, automation systems, alarms, sensors and electronic equipment. The officer diagnoses faults, performs preventive maintenance and supports safe equipment operation.
Key responsibilities include:

items.text: Inspecting and maintaining electrical power-generation and distribution systems.
Troubleshooting motors, switchboards, transformers and electrical control circuits.
Maintaining automation, monitoring, alarm and control systems.
Supporting instrumentation, sensors and process-control equipment.
Maintaining selected navigation, communication and electronic systems within the officer's assigned responsibilities and competence.
Following electrical isolation, lockout/tagout and permit-to-work procedures.
Supporting planned maintenance, inspections and equipment testing.
Maintaining technical records, maintenance reports and spare-parts inventories.
Coordinating with the Chief Engineer, engineering officers and shore-based technical teams.
Responding to electrical faults and equipment emergencies according to shipboard procedures.

rows.text: Electrical fundamentals, electronics, automation and approved maritime training
Shipboard electrical maintenance, fault diagnosis and planned maintenance
Complex automation, high-voltage systems where qualified, technical supervision and reliability
Fleet technical support, electrical systems management, technical audits or superintendent-track roles

blocks.text: These are illustrative horizons, not guaranteed promotion dates. Progress depends on the candidate's education, approved training, sea service, certification, employer and vessel assignments.
Typical pathway

items.text: Complete an eligible electrical, electronics, electrical and electronics, instrumentation or other accepted technical qualification, according to the current approved ETO route.
Verify eligibility for the relevant ETO training programme.
Complete approved pre-sea ETO training and required safety courses.
Complete prescribed onboard training or sea service.
Meet the applicable assessment and certification requirements.
Join a vessel as an ETO when the required qualifications and employment conditions are satisfied.
Build experience in electrical maintenance, automation, troubleshooting and shipboard safety.

blocks.text: Important considerations in India

Before enrolling, verify the latest eligibility requirements, accepted academic qualifications, approved institute status, medical standards, training duration and certification pathway with the Directorate General of Shipping (DG Shipping), India, and the institution.
Do not assume that every electrical or electronics degree automatically qualifies a candidate for ETO training. Approved routes and requirements can differ and may change.
Year 1 — Electrical and Electronics Foundations

blocks.label: Goal
blocks.text: Build the technical foundation required for shipboard electrical work.

rows.text: AC/DC circuits, voltage, current, power and circuit analysis
Transformers, motors, generators and operating principles
Diodes, transistors, rectifiers, amplifiers and power electronics
Algebra, trigonometry, calculus and applied numerical methods
Basic Python or C for logic, data processing and technical exercises
Electrical hazards, PPE, safe working practices and emergency awareness
Circuit diagrams, wiring diagrams and equipment manuals

blocks.text: Suggested projects

items.text: Build and test low-voltage circuits using appropriate supervision.
Create a basic motor-control circuit simulation.
Prepare a digital electrical maintenance log.
Practise reading wiring diagrams and electrical schematics.

blocks.text: Year 2 — Electrical Machines, Controls and Instrumentation

blocks.label: Goal
blocks.text: Develop applied skills in industrial electrical systems.

rows.text: Motor starters, protection, transformers and generator fundamentals
Distribution, switchgear, circuit breakers and protective devices
Feedback control, relays, contactors and control logic
Sensors, transducers, measurement and calibration principles
PLC fundamentals, input/output signals and troubleshooting logic
Digital electronics, power supplies and electronic control circuits
Inspection schedules, fault logs and preventive maintenance

blocks.text: Suggested projects

items.text: Simulate a motor-starting and protection system.
Develop a PLC-based tank-level or pump-control simulation.
Create a fault-diagnosis chart for common electrical problems.
Build a basic sensor-monitoring project.

blocks.text: Year 3 — Maritime Electrical Systems and Applied Automation

blocks.label: Goal
blocks.text: Connect electrical engineering knowledge to shipboard equipment.

rows.text: Generator distribution, switchboards and power-management principles
Pumps, motors, lighting, emergency power and auxiliary systems
Alarm monitoring, control systems and machinery instrumentation
Principles of radar, electronic charts, positioning and related equipment
Maritime communication fundamentals and equipment interfaces
Electrical isolation, safe testing, risk assessment and emergency procedures
Planned maintenance systems, technical records and spares management

blocks.text: Suggested projects

items.text: Develop a shipboard electrical-system block diagram.
Simulate generator load sharing or power-management logic.
Create an alarm-and-sensor monitoring dashboard.
Prepare a maintenance plan for a hypothetical shipboard motor system.

blocks.text: These are educational exercises. Actual shipboard equipment work must follow approved procedures and be carried out under qualified supervision.
Year 4 — ETO Preparation and Professional Readiness

blocks.label: Goal
blocks.text: Prepare for approved maritime training, assessments and shipboard responsibilities.

rows.text: Systematic fault identification and safe diagnostic procedures
Protection coordination, switchboard operation and electrical reliability
PLCs, control systems, sensors, alarms and monitoring
Applicable STCW training and shipboard safety procedures
Work orders, inspection schedules, equipment history and spare parts
Fault reports, maintenance records and handover documentation

blocks.label: Graduation target
blocks.text: Establish the academic and technical foundation required for the approved ETO pathway, and identify all remaining training, sea-service and certification requirements.
A four-year academic roadmap does not itself confer ETO certification; the approved route and required practical training must be completed.

Supports automated machinery and control systems

blocks.text: Safety-critical work must follow the vessel's procedures, equipment manuals and applicable electrical-safety requirements. Isolation and testing must never be bypassed to save time.

blocks.text: Use safe, low-voltage prototypes or simulations for student projects. Do not build or test hazardous high-voltage systems without suitable facilities and qualified supervision.
For the ETO career path, prioritize relevant electrical experience and approved maritime training over unrelated internships.
Recommended steps

items.text: Confirm that your academic qualification is accepted for the intended ETO route.
Compare approved training institutes, course requirements, total costs and placement arrangements.
Build experience with motors, switchgear, instrumentation, automation and electrical maintenance.
Seek internships or industrial training in electrical maintenance, automation, control systems or marine electrical services where eligible.
Complete the prescribed pre-sea training and required safety courses.
Secure the required onboard training or sea service through a legitimate arrangement.
Maintain all training records and certificates.
Prepare for competency assessments and employer technical interviews.

blocks.text: Before accepting an offer

items.text: Verify the institute and training programme's approval status.
Confirm who arranges onboard training and how sea service is documented.
Request written details of fees, placement conditions and expected timelines.
Independently verify the shipping company or recruitment agency.
Be cautious of guaranteed-placement promises or demands for unexplained recruitment fees.

blocks.text: Depending on the qualification and applicable maritime eligibility rules, graduates may consider:

items.text: ETO trainee or approved training-route candidate.
Electrical maintenance trainee.
Marine electrical workshop technician.
Industrial electrical maintenance technician.
Automation or instrumentation technician.
PLC and control-system trainee.
Electrical testing and commissioning trainee.
Shipyard electrical technician.
Marine equipment service technician.

blocks.text: These are not interchangeable qualifications. An industrial electrical role does not automatically qualify someone to work as a shipboard ETO.

blocks.text: The required certificate list depends on the approved ETO pathway, vessel assignment, flag state and current regulations. Confirm the current requirements with the relevant maritime authority and approved training provider.
A postgraduate qualification is not usually the first requirement for becoming an ETO. Relevant technical education, approved maritime training, onboard experience and certification take priority.
Potential further-study areas include:

items.text: M.Tech in Electrical Engineering.
M.Tech in Power Systems.
M.Tech in Control Systems or Industrial Automation.
Postgraduate study in marine engineering systems or maritime technology.
Courses in reliability engineering, asset management or technical operations.

blocks.text: A postgraduate degree may help with selected shore-based technical roles, but it does not replace mandatory maritime certification or sea service.

rows.text: Control systems, PLCs, alarms and monitoring
Fault diagnosis, repairs and preventive maintenance
Sensors, measurement, calibration and control loops
Electrical systems on offshore support and specialist vessels
Electronic equipment and associated technical support
Electrical load monitoring and energy optimisation

items: Required Practical Training and Sea Service

blocks.text: The progression beyond ETO varies by employer and may involve a transition to shore-based work. Unlike the deck-officer pathway, the ETO pathway does not normally progress to Master or Captain through the same certification sequence.

blocks.text: By graduation or completion of the relevant technical programme, the candidate should aim to:

items.text: Understand electrical circuits, machines, power systems and electronics.
Demonstrate foundational competence in control systems and instrumentation.
Complete practical projects involving safe fault diagnosis and automation.
Read electrical diagrams and produce clear technical reports.
Understand shipboard electrical hazards and isolation principles.
Identify the approved ETO training and certification pathway.
Verify eligibility, medical requirements and onboard training arrangements.
Be prepared to pursue approved training and entry-level electrical opportunities.

blocks.label: Important distinction
blocks.text: Graduation alone does not qualify a candidate to serve as an ETO. The candidate must satisfy the applicable maritime training, practical experience, certification and employer requirements.

The strongest route to becoming an Electro-Technical Officer is to combine a suitable electrical or electronics qualification with approved maritime training, hands-on troubleshooting experience, shipboard safety competence and the required certification.

For students, the most valuable preparation is to master electrical machines, power distribution, automation, instrumentation and safe diagnostic practices. For long-term progression, build experience with increasingly complex shipboard systems and develop expertise in maintenance reliability, technical documentation and fleet support.
